chapter: Cranial Nerve XI (The Spinal Accessory Nerve)
vignette: A 29-year-old woman undergoes an excisional biopsy of a lymph node in the right posterior cervical triangle. Two weeks later, she notes a dragging sensation, dull aching pain in the right shoulder, and difficulty styling her hair. On examination, the right shoulder droops downwards and outwards. When she abducts her arm in the scapular plane, the right scapula wings with its inferior angle shifting laterally and upwards. Neck rotation against resistance to the left is entirely normal.
question: Why is sternocleidomastoid strength preserved while the trapezius is paralyzed?
options: The spinal accessory nerve supplies the sternocleidomastoid muscle in the anterior neck before traversing the posterior triangle to reach the trapezius
The sternocleidomastoid is innervated exclusively by the ansa cervicalis
The biopsy injured the dorsal scapular nerve rather than the accessory nerve
The trapezius muscle is innervated by the cervical plexus roots C1 and C2
The spinal accessory nerve decussates within the posterior triangle

explanation.why_correct: The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) exits the jugular foramen, descends in the anterior neck, and pierces the sternocleidomastoid (SCM) to supply it. It then emerges from the posterior border of the SCM and traverses the posterior cervical triangle obliquely and superficially, covered only by skin and cervical fascia, before entering the anterior border of the trapezius. Lymph node biopsies in the posterior triangle frequently sever the nerve distal to the SCM branches, paralyzing the trapezius (lateral scapular winging, shoulder droop) while leaving the SCM completely intact.
distractors: The ansa cervicalis innervates the strap muscles (omohyoid, sternohyoid, sternothyroid), not the SCM.
The dorsal scapular nerve innervates the rhomboids and levator scapulae; its lesion causes medial scapular winging without shoulder drooping.
The trapezius receives motor innervation from CN XI, while C3-C4 branches provide mainly proprioception.
The spinal accessory nerve does not decussate in the neck.
explanation.key_point: Superficial traversal of the posterior cervical triangle renders the spinal accessory nerve vulnerable to iatrogenic biopsy injury, paralyzing the trapezius while sparing the SCM.

chapter: Cranial Nerve XI (The Spinal Accessory Nerve)
source_quote: In some series, the nerve was most commonly injured by surgical trauma at the time of lymph node biopsy or tumor excision
vignette: A 32-year-old woman undergoes an uncomplicated excisional biopsy of a lymph node in the right posterior cervical triangle. Two weeks later, she complains of a constant dull ache in her right neck and shoulder, and difficulty lifting her right arm above her head to dry her hair. On examination, the right shoulder droops, and the vertebral border of her right scapula flares laterally and downward.
question: Which nerve was most likely injured during this procedure?
options: Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) in the posterior triangle of the neck
Long thoracic nerve of Bell supplying the serratus anterior
Dorsal scapular nerve supplying the rhomboids
Suprascapular nerve in the suprascapular notch
Axillary nerve in the quadrangular space

explanation.why_correct: The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) has a superficial, vulnerable course as it crosses the posterior cervical triangle (between the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid and the anterior border of the trapezius), lying just beneath the investing layer of deep cervical fascia. It is the most frequently injured cranial nerve during minor neck procedures (e.g., lymph node biopsy, branchial cleft cyst excision). Denervation of the trapezius produces shoulder droop, impaired arm abduction above horizontal, and lateral/downward winging of the scapula.
distractors: The long thoracic nerve innervates the serratus anterior; its injury causes MEDIAL winging of the scapula (inferior angle moves medially and posteriorly when pushing against a wall).
The dorsal scapular nerve innervates the rhomboids and levator scapulae; injury causes subtle medial retraction weakness without major shoulder droop.
The suprascapular nerve innervates the supraspinatus and infraspinatus; injury impairs initial 15° abduction and external rotation without trapezius atrophy or shoulder droop.
The axillary nerve innervates the deltoid and teres minor; it is injured in anterior shoulder dislocations or surgical neck humerus fractures.
explanation.key_point: The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) runs superficially across the posterior cervical triangle; iatrogenic injury during lymph node biopsy causes trapezius palsy, shoulder droop, and lateral scapular winging.

chapter: Cranial Nerve XI (The Spinal Accessory Nerve)
source_quote: The right sternocleidomastoid is thus tested by having the patient rotate his or her head to the left against resistance
vignette: A 45-year-old man sustains a high cervical stab wound damaging the right spinal accessory nerve rootlets as they ascend through the foramen magnum. On physical examination, the examiner assesses the sternocleidomastoid (SCM) muscle.
question: Weakness of the right sternocleidomastoid muscle causes impairment in which of the following head movements?
options: Turning the head to the left against resistance
Turning the head to the right against resistance
Extending the neck backwards against resistance
Tucking the chin backward with the head maintained in midline
Tilting the ear toward the left shoulder

explanation.why_correct: The sternocleidomastoid muscle attaches to the mastoid process and the sternum/clavicle. When the RIGHT SCM contracts, it pulls the mastoid forward and downward, rotating the chin to the OPPOSITE (LEFT) side. Therefore, a lesion of the right SCM or right spinal accessory nerve causes weakness in turning the head to the CONTRALATERAL (LEFT) side against manual resistance.
distractors: Turning the head to the right against resistance is performed by the LEFT sternocleidomastoid muscle.
Neck extension is mediated by bilateral splenius capitis, semispinalis, and upper trapezius, not SCM.
Retraction of the chin is performed by deep cervical flexors and suboccipital muscles.
Lateral flexion of the neck tilts the head toward the IPSILATERAL (right) shoulder, while rotating the face to the left.
explanation.key_point: Contraction of the sternocleidomastoid muscle rotates the head to the CONTRALATERAL side; a right CN XI lesion impairs head turning to the left.

chapter: Cranial Nerve XI (The Spinal Accessory Nerve)
section: Central Cortical Control of SCM and Trapezius
vignette: A 64-year-old right-handed woman suffers an acute ischemic stroke of the right cerebral hemisphere involving the precentral motor cortex. On examination, she has left hemiparesis and left lower facial weakness. When her neck musculature is tested, she has difficulty turning her head to the right, while head turning to the left is strong.
question: What neuroanatomical principle governs the supranuclear (cortical) innervation of the sternocleidomastoid muscle?
options: The sternocleidomastoid motor subnucleus receives predominantly ipsilateral (uncrossed) corticobulbar innervation from the motor cortex
The sternocleidomastoid receives purely contralateral crossed corticobulbar innervation like standard limb muscles
The sternocleidomastoid receives no cortical innervation and is driven entirely by spinal cord C1-C4 pacemakers
Both sternocleidomastoid muscles receive bilateral symmetric innervation cancelling all unilateral hemispheric stroke deficits
The sternocleidomastoid is innervated exclusively by the cerebellum without corticospinal input

explanation.why_correct: The corticobulbar control of the SCM is clinically unique: each cerebral hemisphere innervates the IPSILATERAL SCM motor nucleus in the cervical cord (uncrossed). Because the right SCM turns the head to the LEFT, the right cerebral hemisphere normally turns the head to the left (synergistic with the frontal eye field driving leftward gaze and the motor cortex driving the left arm/leg). Therefore, a RIGHT hemispheric stroke paralyzes the right SCM, causing weakness in turning the head to the CONTRALATERAL (LEFT) side, or clinically, the patient's head turns preferentially toward the side of the hemispheric lesion ('looking toward the lesion').
distractors: If SCM received classical crossed innervation, a right hemispheric lesion would paralyze the left SCM, which turns the head to the right, contradicting clinical observation.
The SCM is under voluntary cortical motor control, not autonomous spinal pacemakers.
Bilateral symmetric innervation would produce no head-turning deficit after a unilateral hemispheric stroke.
The SCM receives robust corticobulbar projection, not cerebellar-exclusive control.
explanation.key_point: Supranuclear control of the sternocleidomastoid is IPSILATERAL; a right hemispheric lesion impairs the right SCM, leading to difficulty turning the head to the left.

chapter: Cranial Nerve XI (The Spinal Accessory Nerve)
vignette: A 28-year-old tennis player presents with shoulder asymmetry and fatigue. Physical examination reveals that when the patient's arms are resting by his side, the superior and vertebral borders of the right scapula are displaced laterally, and the shoulder is depressed. When he attempts to abduct the arm laterally, the lateral winging worsens. However, when he performs a wall push-up, there is no medial displacement or posterior flaring of the vertebral border.
question: How does lateral scapular winging (CN XI / trapezius) differ from medial scapular winging (long thoracic nerve / serratus anterior)?
options: Trapezius weakness produces lateral winging accented by arm abduction; serratus anterior weakness produces medial winging accented by arm forward flexion and pushing against resistance
Trapezius weakness produces medial winging with arm forward elevation; serratus weakness causes lateral winging when resting
Both nerves produce identical medial winging, distinguished only by electromyography of the biceps brachii
Trapezius paralysis spares scapular position completely because the rhomboids fully substitute for all trapezius vectors
Serratus anterior winging resolves completely when pushing against a wall

explanation.why_correct: The distinction between trapezius and serratus anterior winging is a high-yield clinical localization point: (1) Trapezius palsy (CN XI) causes LATERAL winging: the vertebral border shifts laterally and the superior angle moves away from the spine; it is accented when abducting the arm laterally in the coronal plane. (2) Serratus anterior palsy (long thoracic nerve) causes MEDIAL winging: the vertebral border moves medially and posterior flaring occurs away from the thoracic wall; it is dramatically accented by pushing against a wall with arms flexed forward in the sagittal plane.
distractors: This reverses the characteristics: trapezius produces lateral winging, not medial winging with forward elevation.
They produce distinct geometric winging patterns (lateral vs medial) clinically evident on exam without relying on biceps EMG.
Rhomboids retract the scapula medially, but cannot substitute for the extensive upward rotation and stabilization of the trapezius.
Serratus anterior winging is maximal and most prominent during wall push-ups, not resolved.
explanation.key_point: Trapezius palsy (CN XI) = lateral scapular winging accentuated by arm abduction; Serratus anterior palsy (long thoracic nerve) = medial scapular winging accentuated by forward pushing.

chapter: Cranial Nerve XI (The Spinal Accessory Nerve)
section: Origin and Course of Spinal Accessory Nerve
source_quote: The spinal part arises from a column of cells (the accessory nucleus) that extend from the first to the sixth cervical cord segments
vignette: A neurosurgeon performs a posterior fossa craniectomy and suboccipital decompression. During exposure of the craniocervical junction and foramen magnum, she identifies the spinal accessory nerve.
question: From where do the motor rootlets that form the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) arise, and what path do they take to exit the skull?
options: Arise from anterior horn cells of C1 to C5-C6 cervical spinal cord, ascend through the foramen magnum into the posterior fossa, and exit through the jugular foramen
Arise from the nucleus ambiguus in the rostral medulla, traverse the internal acoustic meatus, and exit through the stylomastoid foramen
Arise from the spinal trigeminal nucleus in the caudal medulla and exit through the hypoglossal canal
Arise from the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus and exit through the foramen rotundum
Arise from the cuneate nucleus in the lower medulla and exit through the foramen spinosum

explanation.why_correct: The spinal accessory nerve is anatomically unique: its motor neurons arise in the accessory nucleus in the posterolateral part of the anterior horn of the upper cervical spinal cord (segments C1 through C5 or C6). The rootlets emerge from the lateral funiculus of the cord, coalesce into a single ascending trunk that enters the posterior cranial fossa through the foramen magnum, and then exits the skull base through the jugular foramen (pars venosa) alongside CN IX and X.
distractors: The internal acoustic meatus and stylomastoid foramen transmit CN VII and VIII, not CN XI.
The spinal trigeminal nucleus is sensory, not motor, and CN XI exits via the jugular foramen, not the hypoglossal canal.
The dorsal motor nucleus is parasympathetic, and foramen rotundum transmits V2.
The cuneate nucleus is somatic sensory, and foramen spinosum transmits the middle meningeal artery.
explanation.key_point: The spinal accessory nerve originates from upper cervical spinal anterior horns (C1-C5/6), ascends through the foramen magnum, and exits through the jugular foramen.

chapter: Cranial Nerve XI (The Spinal Accessory Nerve)
source_quote: cortical, capsular, and high brainstem lesions affecting corticobulbar fibers may result in decreased strength on the head turning away from the side of the lesion
vignette: A 64-year-old man has an acute right middle cerebral artery infarct involving the cortex and internal capsule, with left hemiparesis. Strength of the neck muscles is tested against resistance.
question: Which finding is expected?
options: Weakness of turning the head to the right
Weakness of bilateral neck flexion with the head tending to fall backward
Weakness of turning the head to the left
Weakness of neck extension with the head tending to fall forward
Normal head turning, because the sternocleidomastoid has purely crossed cortical input

explanation.why_correct: The sternocleidomastoid receives a strong input from the ipsilateral hemisphere, so cortical, capsular and high brainstem lesions weaken head turning away from the side of the lesion. A right hemispheric lesion weakens the right sternocleidomastoid, which turns the head to the left.
distractors: Turning toward the side of the lesion is the movement that is preserved, since it uses the sternocleidomastoid on the opposite side.
Bilateral sternocleidomastoid weakness would make the head fall backward, but a unilateral hemispheric lesion does not produce bilateral weakness.
Head falling forward with weak neck extension indicates bilateral trapezius weakness, not a unilateral hemispheric lesion.
The sternocleidomastoid is not purely crossed; it receives chiefly ipsilateral and partly bilateral cortical input, so weakness is expected.
explanation.key_point: Hemispheric lesions weaken head turning away from the lesion, because sternocleidomastoid control is chiefly ipsilateral.

chapter: Cranial Nerve XI (The Spinal Accessory Nerve)
source_quote: Thus, a ventral pontine lesion can cause supranuclear paresis of the trapezius with sparing of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
vignette: A 66-year-old man has an acute infarct in the left ventral pons with right hemiparesis. He cannot shrug the right shoulder, yet rotates his head against resistance and flexes his neck normally. There is no atrophy or fasciculation of the weak trapezius, and the tongue, palate and voice are normal.
question: Which mechanism best explains the isolated trapezius weakness?
options: Injury to the right spinal accessory nerve in the posterior cervical triangle
Injury to the lower brainstem tegmentum
Interruption of supranuclear fibers to the trapezius, which run ventrally in the brainstem
Injury to the cervical cord at the C1-C2 segments
Injury to the right jugular foramen

explanation.why_correct: The corticobulbar fibers to the sternocleidomastoid lie in the brainstem tegmentum, whereas those to the trapezius lie ventrally. A ventral pontine lesion can therefore cause supranuclear paresis of the trapezius with sparing of the sternocleidomastoid, and without atrophy or fasciculations.
distractors: A distal accessory nerve injury would cause a lower motor neuron trapezius palsy with atrophy and would not explain the hemiparesis.
A lower brainstem tegmental lesion would weaken the sternocleidomastoid while sparing the trapezius, the opposite pattern.
The C1-C2 segments innervate mainly the sternocleidomastoid, so a lesion there would spare the trapezius.
A jugular foramen lesion would also affect cranial nerves IX and X (dysphagia, palatal droop, depressed gag) and weaken the sternocleidomastoid.
explanation.key_point: Supranuclear fibers to the trapezius are ventral, so a ventral pontine lesion weakens the trapezius with the sternocleidomastoid spared.

chapter: Cranial Nerve XI (The Spinal Accessory Nerve)
source_quote: cord levels C1 and C2 innervate predominantly the ipsilateral sternocleidomastoid muscle, and levels C3 and C4 innervate primarily the ipsilateral trapezius
vignette: A 48-year-old man has an intramedullary tumor involving the right ventral horn at the C1 and C2 cord levels. He has atrophy of the right sternocleidomastoid. Shoulder shrug on the right is relatively preserved.
question: What explains this distribution of weakness?
options: The right trapezius is innervated chiefly by C1 and C2
The right sternocleidomastoid is innervated chiefly by the C3 and C4 segments
The C1 and C2 levels innervate chiefly the ipsilateral sternocleidomastoid, whereas C3 and C4 innervate chiefly the ipsilateral trapezius
Both muscles are supplied equally by all segments from C1 to C6
The cranial root of the accessory nerve supplies the sternocleidomastoid

explanation.why_correct: The accessory nucleus is somatotopically arranged: cord levels C1 and C2 innervate predominantly the ipsilateral sternocleidomastoid and levels C3 and C4 innervate primarily the ipsilateral trapezius. A high cervical lesion therefore affects the sternocleidomastoid more than the trapezius.
distractors: This reverses the arrangement; the trapezius is supplied chiefly by C3 and C4.
This reverses the arrangement; the sternocleidomastoid is supplied chiefly by C1 and C2.
The nucleus is arranged somatotopically, not with equal supply of both muscles from all segments.
The cranial root joins the vagus nerve to supply the pharynx and larynx; the spinal root supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius.
explanation.key_point: C1-C2 accessory nucleus segments serve mainly the sternocleidomastoid and C3-C4 serve mainly the trapezius.

chapter: Cranial Nerve XI (The Spinal Accessory Nerve)
source_quote: Bilateral sternocleidomastoid paresis causes weakness of neck flexion, with the head tending to fall backward when the patient attempts to stand erect.
vignette: A 54-year-old man has had bilateral spinal accessory nerve injuries after neck radiation. When he tries to stand erect his head tends to fall backward, and he cannot flex his neck against pressure on his forehead.
question: Which muscles are paretic?
options: Both trapezius muscles
Both sternocleidomastoid muscles
The right sternocleidomastoid only
The left trapezius only
Both cricothyroid muscles

explanation.why_correct: Bilateral sternocleidomastoid paresis causes weakness of neck flexion, with the head tending to fall backward when the patient attempts to stand erect.
distractors: Bilateral trapezius paresis causes weakness of neck extension, with the head tending to fall forward.
A unilateral sternocleidomastoid lesion does not alter head position at rest and mainly weakens turning to the opposite side.
A unilateral trapezius lesion causes shoulder droop and weakness of shrugging, not a bilateral neck flexion deficit.
The cricothyroid is a laryngeal muscle supplied by the superior laryngeal nerve, not a neck flexor.
explanation.key_point: Bilateral sternocleidomastoid paresis makes the head fall backward; bilateral trapezius paresis makes it fall forward.

chapter: Cranial Nerve XI (The Spinal Accessory Nerve)
source_quote: Garcin (hemibase syndrome) All cranial nerves on one side (often incomplete)
vignette: A 55-year-old man with nasopharyngeal carcinoma develops progressive, incomplete palsies of cranial nerves on the right side, from facial numbness to tongue weakness. Imaging shows an infiltrative mass arising from the base of the skull.
question: Which named syndrome does this represent?
options: Vernet syndrome
Collet-Sicard syndrome
Tapia syndrome
Garcin syndrome
Schmidt syndrome

explanation.why_correct: Garcin (hemibase) syndrome involves all cranial nerves on one side, often incompletely, from an infiltrative lesion arising from the base of the skull, especially nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
distractors: Vernet syndrome involves only cranial nerves IX, X and XI at the jugular foramen.
Collet-Sicard syndrome involves cranial nerves IX, X, XI and XII, usually in the retroparotid space.
Tapia syndrome involves cranial nerves X and XII, usually high in the neck.
Schmidt syndrome involves only cranial nerves X and XI.
explanation.key_point: Garcin (hemibase) syndrome is a unilateral palsy of most or all cranial nerves, typically from skull base nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

chapter: Cranial Nerve XI (The Spinal Accessory Nerve)
source_quote: Villaret syndrome (affecting cranial nerves IX, X, XI, and XII, the sympathetic chain, and occasionally cranial nerve VII)
vignette: A 49-year-old woman has a carotid artery dissection with an associated aneurysm at the skull base. She has ipsilateral hoarseness, dysphagia, trapezius and sternocleidomastoid weakness and tongue weakness with atrophy. She also has ipsilateral ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis.
question: Which syndrome best matches these findings?
options: Collet-Sicard syndrome
Vernet syndrome
Villaret syndrome
Jackson syndrome
Schmidt syndrome

explanation.why_correct: Villaret syndrome affects cranial nerves IX, X, XI and XII plus the sympathetic chain (and occasionally VII), usually from a retroparotid or retropharyngeal lesion; it has been described with carotid artery dissection and aneurysm. The ipsilateral Horner syndrome marks sympathetic chain involvement.
distractors: Collet-Sicard syndrome involves the same four lower cranial nerves but not the sympathetic chain, so there is no Horner syndrome.
Vernet syndrome involves only IX, X and XI, sparing the tongue and the sympathetic chain.
Jackson syndrome involves X, XI and XII without IX and without Horner syndrome.
Schmidt syndrome involves only X and XI.
explanation.key_point: Lower cranial neuropathies IX-XII plus Horner syndrome indicate Villaret syndrome.

chapter: Cranial Nerve XI (The Spinal Accessory Nerve)
source_quote: Jackson Cranial nerves X, XI, and XII May be intraparenchymal (medulla)
vignette: A 59-year-old man with a lesion in the medulla has right vocal cord paralysis with palatal droop, weakness of the right trapezius and sternocleidomastoid, and right tongue weakness with deviation to the right. Taste over the posterior third of the tongue and pharyngeal sensation are normal.
question: Which named syndrome best fits?
options: Collet-Sicard syndrome
Tapia syndrome
Schmidt syndrome
Vernet syndrome
Jackson syndrome

explanation.why_correct: Jackson syndrome involves cranial nerves X, XI and XII. It may be intraparenchymal in the medulla, or usually intracranial before the nerves leave the skull. IX is spared in this patient, as shown by normal taste and pharyngeal sensation.
distractors: Collet-Sicard syndrome also involves cranial nerve IX, which would cause loss of posterior tongue taste and pharyngeal sensory loss.
Tapia syndrome involves only X and XII, which would not explain the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid weakness.
Schmidt syndrome involves only X and XI and would not cause tongue weakness.
Vernet syndrome involves IX, X and XI and spares the tongue.
explanation.key_point: Jackson syndrome is the combination of cranial nerves X, XI and XII.

chapter: Cranial Nerve XI (The Spinal Accessory Nerve)
source_quote: Neuromyotonia of accessory nerve, characterized by transient involuntary tonic contractures of the sternocleidomastoid muscle with head movements, has been described after radiation therapy
vignette: A 58-year-old man treated with neck radiation for cancer years ago has episodes in which his right neck muscle contracts involuntarily during head movements. The muscle is hypertrophied and is slow to relax after each contraction.
question: Which disorder best explains this presentation?
options: Dropped head syndrome from neck extensor myopathy
Neuromyotonia of the accessory nerve
Stretch injury of the accessory nerve in the posterior triangle
Jugular foramen syndrome
Neurogenic atrophy of the trapezius

explanation.why_correct: Neuromyotonia of the accessory nerve is characterized by transient involuntary tonic contractures of the sternocleidomastoid with head movements, with muscle hypertrophy and delayed relaxation, and has been described after radiation therapy.
distractors: Dropped head syndrome is weakness of neck extension, not involuntary tonic contractions with hypertrophy.
A stretch injury causes weakness and atrophy of the muscle, not tonic contractions with delayed relaxation.
Jugular foramen syndrome causes paresis and atrophy of the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius with IX and X signs.
Neurogenic atrophy of the trapezius is a weakness syndrome, whereas this patient has overactivity of a hypertrophied muscle.
explanation.key_point: Postradiation accessory nerve neuromyotonia causes tonic sternocleidomastoid contractions with hypertrophy and delayed relaxation.

chapter: Cranial Nerve XI (The Spinal Accessory Nerve)
source_quote: hemiplegia associated with ipsilateral (to the hemiplegia) sternocleidomastoid paresis implies a lesion at or below the pontine level
vignette: A 62-year-old man has a dense left hemiplegia. On examination the left sternocleidomastoid is also paretic: he is weak when turning his head to the right. This is the same side as the hemiplegia.
question: Where is the lesion most likely located?
options: In the right cerebral hemisphere above the double decussation of the pathway
At or below the pontine level
In the right internal capsule only
In the left jugular foramen
In the right frontal eye field

explanation.why_correct: Sternocleidomastoid control is thought to cross to the opposite pons and return to the cord side ipsilateral to the hemisphere of origin. Hemiplegia with sternocleidomastoid paresis on the SAME side as the hemiplegia therefore implies a lesion at or below the pontine level, after the first decussation. When the paretic muscle is contralateral to the hemiplegia, a hemispheric lesion is likely.
distractors: A hemispheric lesion would paralyze the sternocleidomastoid ipsilateral to the lesion, which is contralateral to the hemiplegia.
A capsular lesion behaves like a hemispheric one, with the weak sternocleidomastoid opposite the hemiplegic side.
A jugular foramen lesion would cause lower cranial nerve signs and trapezius weakness, but would not cause hemiplegia.
A frontal eye field lesion causes gaze and head deviation effects, not hemiplegia with ipsilateral sternocleidomastoid paresis.
explanation.key_point: Hemiplegia with ipsilateral sternocleidomastoid paresis suggests a lesion at or below the pons.

chapter: Cranial Nerve XI (The Spinal Accessory Nerve)
source_quote: cause contraction of the ipsilateral sternocleidomastoid muscle as the head turns to the side contralateral to the epileptogenic lesion
vignette: A 35-year-old woman has a focal seizure in which her head turns to the left, with contraction of the right sternocleidomastoid muscle. An epileptogenic lesion in areas 8 and 9 of the cortex is suspected.
question: On which side is the epileptogenic lesion most likely located?
options: The left cerebral hemisphere, ipsilateral to the head turning
The left medulla
The right cerebral hemisphere, contralateral to the head turning
The right jugular foramen
The left cervical cord

explanation.why_correct: Focal seizures arising in areas 8 and 9 cause contraction of the ipsilateral sternocleidomastoid muscle, so the head turns to the side contralateral to the epileptogenic lesion. Right sternocleidomastoid contraction turns the head to the left, so the focus is in the right hemisphere.
distractors: The head turns away from the epileptogenic hemisphere, so a left focus would turn the head to the right.
The medulla is not a site of cortical adversive seizures; the cortical areas involved are 8 and 9.
The jugular foramen is a peripheral lesion site that would cause weakness, not ictal head turning.
A cervical cord lesion would cause weakness or atrophy, not a seizure with head turning.
explanation.key_point: Adversive seizures contract the ipsilateral sternocleidomastoid and turn the head away from the epileptogenic hemisphere.
